clinician.trajectory_summary: A 70-year-old white British female with asthma and hypothyroidism presented to the emergency department via ambulance after falling onto an aga the previous day. She presented with right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath. Initial vital signs were normal at triage; oxygen saturation was 90% on high-flow oxygen in the resuscitation room. Physical examination revealed rapidly progressive subcutaneous emphysema with palpable crepitus affecting the head, neck, chest, upper limbs, and abdomen, with palpebral closure, vocal changes, and stridor. Ambulance crew had noted a global pleural rub and wheeze. The patient required rapid sequence intubation. CT imaging confirmed bilateral moderate-volume pneumothoraces (right and left) with associated pulmonary injuries: right lower-lobe hemorrhage and left lower-lobe laceration with collapse. Rib fractures of ribs 7, 8, and 9 in two places on the right side were identified. Bilateral 28Fr chest drains were inserted immediately post-CT, initially draining air; the procedure was technically challenging due to 10–15 cm of edematous tissue overlying the ribs, requiring a second operator. Ventilatory pressures decreased commensurately after drain insertion. The patient remained ventilated and sedated for 3 days in the ICU, with successful extubation and chest drain removal without complications. She was discharged on hospital day 12 with analgesia. At 1-month follow-up, recovery was good with return to usual activities, though with some tiredness and generalized weakness that improved over several months. Throughout the clinical course, there was no documented hemodynamic instability or signs of tension physiology, despite the bilateral pneumothoraces and extensive subcutaneous emphysema.
